source_text: Fiducia Christianorum, resurrectio mortuorum. Illa credentes sumus; hoc credere veritas cogit. Veritatem Deus aperit; sed vulgus irridet, existimans nihil superesse post mortem; et tamen defunctis parentant, et quidem impensissimo officio, pro moribus eorum, pro temporibus esculentorum; ut quos negant sentire quicquam, escam desiderare praesumant. At ego magis ridebo vulgus, tunc quoque, cum ipsos defunctos atrocissime exurit, quos postmodum gulosissime nutrit, iisdem ignibus et promerens et offendens. O pietatem de crudelitate ludentem! sacrificat, an insultat, cum crematis cremat? Plane cum vulgo interdum et sapientes sententiam suam jungunt. Nihil esse post mortem Epicuri schola est. Ait et Seneca, omnia post mortem finiri, etiam ipsam. Satis est autem, si non minor philosophia Pythagorae et Empedocli. Sed et Platonici immortalem animam e contrario reclamant: imo adhuc proxime etiam in corpora remeabilem affirmant; etsi non in eadem, etsi non in humana tantummodo; ut Euphorbus in Pythagoram, Homerus in pavum recenseantur. Certe recidivatum animae corporalem pronuntiaverunt; tolerabilius mutata, quam negata qualitate: pulsata saltem, licet non adita veritate. Ita saeculum resurrectionem mortuorum, nec cum errat, ignorat.
pass_a_gloss: The confidence of Christians is the resurrection of the dead; we are believers in that; this truth compels us to believe; God reveals the truth; but the crowd ridicules, thinking nothing remains after death; and yet they pay their respects to the dead, and indeed with very expensive duty, according to their customs, at the times of feasting; so that they presume those whom they deny feel anything to desire food; but I will laugh at the crowd even more, then also, when it most atrociously burns the very dead, whom afterwards it most greedily nourishes, both earning and offending with the same fires; oh, the piety playing with cruelty; does it sacrifice, or does it insult, when it burns the cremated; plainly even the wise sometimes join their opinion with the crowd; the school of Epicurus is that nothing exists after death; and Seneca says that all things, even the soul itself, end after death; but it is enough if not lesser philosophy, that of Pythagoras and Empedocles; and the Platonists, on the contrary, claim the soul is immortal; indeed they even affirm that it is reborn into bodies; although not into the same ones, although not only into human ones; so that Euphorbus is reckoned into Pythagoras, and Homer into a peacock; certainly they have proclaimed the soul's rebirth into a body; more tolerable with a changed quality, than with a denied one; at least struck, even if not approached by truth; thus the age, even when it errs, does not ignore the resurrection of the dead

pass_b_english: The confidence of Christians rests on the resurrection of the dead; we are believers in that, and this truth compels us to believe. God reveals the truth, but the crowd ridicules it, thinking nothing survives death—and yet they pay their respects to the dead, and at great expense, following their customs and timing their feasts so that they presume the very people they claim feel nothing still desire food. I will laugh at the crowd even more when it atrociously burns the dead, only to gorge on them afterward, both earning and offending with the same fires. Oh, the piety playing with cruelty: does it sacrifice, or does it insult, when it burns the cremated? Plainly, even the wise sometimes join their opinion to the crowd's. The Epicurean school teaches that nothing exists after death. Seneca says the same—that everything ends after death, even the soul itself. But the philosophy of Pythagoras and Empedocles is no lesser authority. The Platonists, by contrast, claim the soul is immortal; indeed, they even affirm it is reborn into bodies—though not the same ones, and not only human ones—so that Euphorbus is reckoned into Pythagoras, and Homer into a peacock. They have certainly proclaimed the soul's rebirth into a body; a changed quality is more tolerable than a denied one: at least struck, even if not reached by truth. Thus the age, even when it errs, does not ignore the resurrection of the dead.

review.notes: Checked paragraph 1. Pass A and Pass B both accurately reflect the Latin text. Pass B provides a more fluent rendering of 'impensissimo officio' as 'at great expense' and 'gulosissime nutrit' as 'gorge on them afterward', which is consistent with the Latin sense. The translation of 'saeculum' as 'the age' and 'parentant' as 'pay their respects' is appropriate. No omissions or errors in scripture or doctrine found.
